questions.title: What does 'procedural right in vacuo' mean in the context of Article III standing?
questions.question_body: I'm reading the section where the court discusses AFL's claim that the OSC violated its procedural right to an investigation under section 1216. The court says that a 'deprivation of a procedural right without some concrete interest that is affected... is insufficient' for standing. Can someone explain what a 'procedural right in vacuo' is? If the statute specifically says the OSC 'shall' conduct an investigation, isn't that a right? Why does the court require a 'concrete interest' on top of that right?

questions.title: How does the court define 'speculative' causation when multiple independent agencies are involved?
questions.question_body: The court rejects AFL's first standing theory because the causal chain is 'too speculative and attenuated.' The chain involves OSC investigating, the MSPB potentially sanctioning employees, and then the DOJ potentially producing records. The court says we can't rely on the 'unfettered choices' of the MSPB and DOJ. Does this mean that if a causal chain involves more than one independent government agency, it is automatically too speculative to satisfy the 'redressability' requirement of standing?

questions.title: How does the court distinguish between the 'mandatory' duty of Section 1216 and the 'discretionary' procedure of Section 1214?
questions.question_body: I'm confused by the interaction between these two statutes. The district court suggested that Section 1216 mandates an investigation, but the appellate court notes that the procedure for that investigation (the notices/information from Section 1214) is discretionary. How can a statute create a mandatory requirement for an action (investigation) while leaving the manner in which that action is performed (notice requirements) up to the agency's discretion? How does this affect a plaintiff's ability to seek a judicial order?

questions.title: Why does an interest in the 'fruits' of a government investigation fail to constitute a 'concrete' informational injury?
questions.question_body: AFL argued that they have an informational interest in the notices and information they would receive if the OSC conducted the investigation. The court held that because Section 1216 doesn't create an 'entitlement' to receive that information, it isn't a 'concrete' injury. Is the court saying that 'informational standing' is only granted if the statute explicitly guarantees the plaintiff will receive specific documents, rather than just granting the agency the power to provide them?

questions.title: Why did the court 'vacate and remand' for lack of jurisdiction instead of simply dismissing the appeal?
questions.question_body: The court concludes that AFL lacks Article III standing, which is a matter of subject-matter jurisdiction. Since the court found that the district court never had the power to hear the case in the first place, why is the proper move to 'vacate and remand with instructions to dismiss' rather than just issuing a final judgment dismissing the appeal? I'm trying to understand the procedural distinction between a merits-based dismissal and a jurisdictional vacatur.
